name: met-stjohn-1856-colosseum
note: Jane Martha St. John, 'The Colosseum', 1856, albumen silver print from paper negative, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gilman Collection, acc. 2005.100.382 (68), https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/287727 . Met Open Access, isPublicDomain true in the Met collection API (CC0); the HTML record page answers 429 to curl so the licence was read from the API flag, not the page. 3821x3005 JPEG, upright, no rotation. Outer wall of the arcades photographed at close range from a short distance; piers and parapet bands are covered in dark pits and slots, clearly visible at 100%. Best image for the film. Crop [40,30,3790,2960] drops the paper margin. The upper-right corner holds part of a roof and the right edge a lamp bracket

name: met-jones-1846-colosseum-second-view
note: Calvert Richard Jones, '67. Colosseum, Rome, Second View', May 1846, salted paper print from paper negative, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Bequest of Maurice B. Sendak, acc. 2013.159.34, https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/306254 . Met Open Access, isPublicDomain true in the API (CC0). 3364x2795, upright. Earliest photograph in the set. Wide view of the outer wall with the tall intact curve at left and the broken stretch at right; rows of small pits on the surviving outer wall piers (right half) at 100%. Handwritten caption along the bottom edge. Crop [150,90,3280,2570]. A man in a top hat and a woman sit at lower centre

name: met-unknown-1850s-colosseum-269024
note: Unknown photographer, '[Colosseum, Rome]', 1850s, salted paper print from paper negative, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, David Hunter McAlpin Fund, acc. 46.1.78, https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/269024 . Met Open Access, isPublicDomain true in the API (CC0). 2778x3513, upright (portrait). Frontal view of the outer wall with all four storeys and the tall surviving outer-wall fragment; holes show only faintly (small dots on piers of the lower arcade), so it works as a whole-building shot, not for magnification. Crop [150,130,2640,3400] drops the black mount edges

name: met-piranesi-1776-veduta-colosseo
note: Giovanni Battista Piranesi, 'Veduta dell'Anfiteatro Flavio detto il Colosseo', from Vedute di Roma, 1776, etching, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Elisha Whittelsey Fund 1959, acc. 59.570.426, https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/360270 . Met Open Access, isPublicDomain true in the API (CC0). 3757x2638, upright. Bird's-eye view of the whole ruin with the arena, legend panels at the bottom corners. Opening shot candidate. Shows the building as it stood, but the holes are not rendered as holes at this scale

name: met-piranesi-1748-anfiteatro-flavio
note: Giovanni Battista Piranesi, 'Plate 12: Anfiteatro Flavio detto il Colosseo in Roma', ca. 1748, etching, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Harris Brisbane Dick Fund 1937, acc. 37.45.3(79), https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/365360 . Met Open Access, isPublicDomain true in the API (CC0). 3994x2010, upright. Exterior of the whole oval with the Arch of Constantine at right; engraved title and 'Piranesi fecit Tav. 12' under the image. Crop [40,50,3955,1840]. No holes depicted

name: met-piranesi-1756-antichita-III-tav53
note: Giovanni Battista Piranesi, 'Means by which the large blocks of travertine and marble were lifted during the construction of the large Tomb of Caecilia Metella', tome 3, tavola 53 from Le Antichita Romane, published 1756-57, etching, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund, acc. 41.71.1.3(53), https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/360365 . Met Open Access, isPublicDomain true in the API (CC0). 3857x3406, upright. Iron lifting hooks and lewis-type irons, the square lifting holes cut in travertine blocks, a crane. It shows iron tools and holes in Roman travertine masonry, NOT joint clamps and not the Colosseum; use only as a loose 'Romans worked travertine with iron' picture

name: met-constant-1848-52-colosseo
note: Eugene Constant, 'Colosseo (Anfiteatro di Flavio)', 1848-52, salted paper print from glass negative, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gilman Collection, acc. 2005.100.799 (29), https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/288424 . Met Open Access, isPublicDomain true in the API (CC0). Only 1743x1299 (below the 3000 px target). Clean whole-building view with a strip of foreground ruin. Low-resolution fallback for the opening

name: suaresius-1651-p4
note: Giuseppe Maria Suares (Suaresius), Diatriba de foraminibus lapidum in priscis aedificiis, Rome 1651, Internet Archive bub_gb_q1SlcBKcJjgC (Google Books scan, National Central Library of Rome), scan 0003 = printed page 4, https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_q1SlcBKcJjgC . Rights: Public Domain Mark 1.0 (licenseurl on the item; a 1651 book). 2500x3575 JPEG2000, upright. Latin page that discusses the holes in the 'Amphitheatrum Titi' (the Colosseum): quotes Donati that the lower piers and arches are marked with many holes, ascribed by some to the Goths, and gives the market-stall (nundinae) explanation; a 'Digitized by Google' mark sits at the lower right. Crop [350,120,1300,3000] for the text block. Copy bub_gb_DYt4WNOy6wEC (1652 edition) is a second scan

name: suaresius-1651-p2
note: Same book and copy, scan 0001 = printed page 2. Public Domain Mark 1.0. 1724x2500, upright. Opens with the question people asked in Rome: why the big Tiburtine stones of the Amphitheatre, squared and polished, are pitted on the outer face with many holes ('crebris foraminibus'); rejects the earthquake story and says the holes are made by hand and tool. 'Digitized by Google' mark at lower right

name: suaresius-1651-p6
note: Same book and copy, scan 0005 = printed page 6. Public Domain Mark 1.0. 2500x3581, upright. Latin passage on stones held together with iron clamps and lead: 'De Gomphis, id est, clavis ferreis' and 'lapides ... ferreis nexibus, atque clavis colligati'. Names clamps in general, not the Colosseum by name on this page. 'Digitized by Google' mark at lower right

name: middleton-1892-vol2-p87
note: John Henry Middleton, The Remains of Ancient Rome, vol. 2 (London: A. and C. Black, 1892), p. 87, Internet Archive remainsofancient02midd (Robarts, University of Toronto copy), scan 0103, https://archive.org/details/remainsofancient02midd . Public domain (1892; author died 1896). 2391x3644, upright. Text page: the exterior is 'massive travertine ... set without mortar, and each clamped to the next with heavy iron clamps, run with lead', and footnote 3: 'The numerous holes, which disfigure the arcades, were made during the early Middle Ages in attempts to extract the then valuable iron of the clamps'. It is Middleton's 1892 statement, with no evidence given on the page. Crops: body text (the 'each clamped to the next' sentence) [200,560,2250,1250]; footnote 3 [180,2910,2250,3290]
